pages.keyword: how to mouse proof your house
pages.h1Hint: How to Mouse-Proof Your House: A Fall Checklist

heroText.title: Mouse-Proof Your House — 7 entry points + how to seal them (label: FALL CHECKLIST)
items: 1. Gaps around pipes — Where plumbing & utilities enter; the #1 mouse door.
2. Under exterior doors — Garage doors especially. If light shows, mice fit.
3. Dryer & exhaust vents — Unscreened vents are open invitations.
4. Foundation cracks — Even hairline cracks widen with frost.
5. Siding-to-foundation gap — That shadow line along the house base.
6. Roofline & chimney — Mice climb. Check soffits, eaves, flashing.
7. Cable & wire holes — AC lines, cable TV, old drill holes.
THE 1/4-INCH RULE: If a pencil fits, a mouse fits. Seal anything wider than 6 mm.
SEAL IT RIGHT: Pack coarse steel wool tight into the gap. Cover with silicone caulk or cement. Mice can't chew through the metal fibers.
TRAP PLACEMENT: Snap traps along walls — mice hug baseboards. Trigger end faces the wall, bait: peanut butter. Check daily. More traps = faster results.
Footer: Safety: keep snap traps where kids & pets can't reach. Never use poison indoors — mice die in walls.

pages.scope: A fall exclusion guide. The 7 entry points mice use most (write them as a numbered list that matches a house diagram: utility and pipe penetrations, gaps under exterior doors, the garage door corners, dryer and other vents, the foundation and sill plate, weep holes and siding gaps, the roofline and soffits), with the gap size that lets a mouse through in inches. A step-by-step steel wool and caulk how-to for small holes and what to use for larger ones (hardware cloth, metal flashing, cement), following CDC's seal-up guidance. A trap placement guide for the mice already inside. Why fall is the season. A printable exclusion checklist as a card block. Pet and child safety for traps and for any bait.

pages.h1Hint: Homemade Ant Killer: 4 Recipes With Exact Ratios

heroText.title: Ant Killer Recipes — 4 tested recipes with exact ratios (label: DIY PEST CONTROL)
items: 1. Borax Sugar Bait — 1 tsp borax : 3 tsp sugar : 2 tbsp warm water. Dissolve, soak cotton balls, set in bottle caps along ant trails. Ants carry it back to the colony. Safety tag MODERATE: Borax is toxic if eaten — enclosed stations only, away from kids & pets.

2. Baking Soda + Sugar — 1 tbsp baking soda : 1 tbsp powdered sugar. Mix dry, sprinkle in shallow lids near entry points. Reapply after 3 days if ants persist. Safety tag LOW: Food-grade ingredients — still keep lids out of pet reach.

3. Vinegar Trail-Breaker — 1 cup white vinegar : 1 cup water. Spray directly on trails, entry points and nests. Wipes out the scent trail ants follow. Safety tag LOW: Safe around kids & pets. Avoid marble/stone — vinegar etches it.

4. Dish Soap Knockdown — 1 tsp dish soap : 1 cup water. Spray directly on visible ants. Breaks surface tension — kills on contact, not the colony. Safety tag LOW: Safe once dry. Scouts only — pair with a bait for the colony.
Footer: Safety first: label every bait, wash hands after handling, and never place borax where children or pets can reach it.

pages.scope: Three or four homemade ant killer recipes, each taken from a university extension or other authoritative source and given with EXACT measurements in US kitchen units: a borax and sugar liquid bait, a borax protein or grease bait for ants that ignore sugar, a vinegar and water trail-breaker for cleanup, and soapy water as a contact spray if a source supports it. Use one recipe block per recipe. For every recipe state what it does and does not do, how long it takes, and a pet and child safety tier with the reason. pages.h1Hint: Signs of Bed Bugs: A 7-Point Checklist to Run Tonight

heroText.title: 7 Signs of Bed Bugs — Grab a flashlight, check tonight (label: INSPECTION GUIDE)
items: 1. Rusty-red stains — On sheets & pillowcases; crushed bugs leave reddish smears. LOOK: Mattress top, seams.
2. Dark ink-like spots — Fecal marks, bleed into fabric like a marker dot. LOOK: Mattress seams, box spring.
3. Shed skins — Pale yellow empty shells, ~1mm; bugs molt 5 times. LOOK: Crevices, behind headboard.
4. Live bugs — Apple-seed sized, flat, reddish-brown ovals. LOOK: Seams, tufts, bed frame joints.
5. Tiny white eggs — Grain-of-rice sized, sticky, hidden in cracks. LOOK: Stitching, screw holes.
6. Musty sweet odor — Coriander-like smell in heavy infestations. LOOK: Whole room — trust your nose.
7. Bite lines — Clusters or zigzags on exposed skin overnight. LOOK: Arms, neck, ankles — morning check.
FIRST 24 HOURS: Don't sleep elsewhere — you'll spread them. Strip the bed: wash HOT, dry on HIGH 30+ min. Declutter around the bed so there's nowhere to hide.
Footer: Found 2+ signs? Don't use bug bombs — they scatter bed bugs deeper. Call a pro for heat treatment.

pages.scope: A 7-point checklist of the physical signs, ranked from strongest evidence to weakest: live bugs, dark fecal spots that smear, shed skins, eggs and eggshells, rusty or reddish blood smears on sheets, a sweet musty odor in heavier infestations, and bites (the weakest sign on their own, per CDC and EPA). For each sign: what it looks like, where to look, and what it is confused with. A 'check tonight' routine with a flashlight and a card, in order, taking about 10 minutes. pages.h1Hint: Tick Identification Chart: Deer Tick vs Dog Tick vs Lone Star Tick

heroText.title: Tick Identification Chart — Know which tick bit you, it matters (label: ONTARIO FIELD GUIDE)
items: ACTUAL SIZE (unfed adults): Deer tick = poppy seed. Lone star = sesame seed. Dog tick = apple seed. Note: engorged (fed) ticks swell to 3x this size.
Black-legged (Deer) tick — LOOKS LIKE: Reddish body, black legs. DISEASES: Lyme disease + anaplasmosis. ONTARIO RANGE: Widespread across southern Ontario.
American Dog tick — LOOKS LIKE: Brown with white markings, larger. DISEASES: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (rare in ON). ONTARIO RANGE: Grassy fields & trails province-wide.
Lone Star tick — LOOKS LIKE: Females: single white dot on back. DISEASES: Ehrlichiosis + alpha-gal (red-meat allergy). ONTARIO RANGE: Moving into southern Ontario.
IF BITTEN — DO THIS: Fine-tipped tweezers, steady upward pull — no twisting. Clean the bite with soap & water or alcohol. Watch 30 days for rash, fever, fatigue — see a doctor if any appear.

TICK-CHECK ROUTINE AFTER THE TRAIL: 1 Shower within 2 hours of coming inside. 2 Full-body check: armpits, groin, hairline, behind ears, waistband. 3 Tumble dry clothes on HIGH 10 min — kills missed ticks. 4 Save any attached tick in a baggie for ID if symptoms appear.
Footer: Remove attached ticks with fine-tipped tweezers, steady upward pull. Watch for rash/fever — see a doctor.

pages.h1Hint: Pet-Safe Pest Control: What Is Lower-Risk for Cats and Dogs

heroText.title: Pet-Safe Pest Control — What's safe around cats & dogs, remedy by remedy (label: VET-AWARE GUIDE)
items: Borax baits — Cats: UNSAFE. Dogs: UNSAFE. Toxic if eaten. Enclosed stations only, locked away.
Peppermint oil — Cats: UNSAFE. Dogs: CAUTION. Cats lack the liver enzyme for phenols — never diffuse near cats.
Diatomaceous earth — Cats: CAUTION. Dogs: CAUTION. Food-grade only. Respiratory irritant — apply when pets are out.
Citronella oil — Cats: CAUTION. Dogs: CAUTION. Dilute heavily. Watch for drooling or pawing at face.
Cedarwood oil — Cats: SAFER. Dogs: SAFER. Among the gentlest options — still dilute, still ventilate.
White vinegar — Cats: SAFE. Dogs: SAFE. Food-safe. Avoid eyes; the smell fades fast.
Snap traps — Cats: CAUTION. Dogs: CAUTION. Place inside walls/attic — never where paws can reach.
Ultrasonic repellers — Cats: SAFE. Dogs: SAFE. No chemicals. Effectiveness varies — it's a supplement.
THE VET RULE: Ask your vet before using ANY essential oil around pets — especially cats. When in doubt, choose the mechanical fix.
Footer: This guide is informational, not veterinary advice. If a pet ingests any pesticide, call your vet or poison control.

pages.h1Hint: Natural Garden Pest Control: A Season-by-Season Guide

heroText.title: Natural Garden Pest Control — Companion planting + pollinator rules + seasonal calendar (label: THE EVERGREEN HUB)
items: COMPANION PLANTING CHART: Marigolds — REPELS aphids, whiteflies, root nematodes; plant along veggie borders & tomato rows. Basil — REPELS flies, mosquitoes, tomato hornworm; beside tomatoes, they help each other. Mint — REPELS ants, aphids, flea beetles; POTS ONLY, mint spreads aggressively. Nasturtiums — REPELS aphids (trap crop); sacrificial planting at garden edges. Lavender — REPELS moths, fleas, mosquitoes; pathways & patio borders.

POLLINATOR-SAFE RULES: 1 Spray at dusk — bees are home asleep. 2 Never spray open blooms, only foliage. 3 Choose targeted insecticidal soap over broad-spectrum killers. 4 Leave some 'wild corners' — predators need habitat too.
SEASONAL CALENDAR: SPRING — Prep soil, plant companions early. SUMMER — Monitor weekly, release beneficials. FALL — Cleanup = fewer overwintering pests. WINTER — Plan rotations, order seeds.

BENEFICIAL INSECTS TO WELCOME: Ladybugs — EATS aphids, mites, whitefly eggs. Lacewings — EATS aphids, thrips, mealybugs. Hoverflies — EATS aphid colonies; larvae feast. Parasitic wasps — EATS aphids, caterpillars (tiny, don't sting).
Footer: Safety: even natural sprays can irritate skin & eyes. Dusk application protects bees; store products from kids & pets.

pages.keyword: how to get rid of fungus gnats
pages.h1Hint: How to Get Rid of Fungus Gnats: The Full Kill Chain

heroText.title: Fungus Gnat Kill Chain — 5 steps, break the breeding cycle (label: HOUSEPLANT RESCUE)
items: 1. LET THE SOIL DRY — Water only when the top 2 inches are dry. Gnat larvae need constant moisture; dryness kills the nursery. NOTE: No product needed. #1 step — skip it and nothing else works.
2. YELLOW STICKY TRAPS — Stake 1 trap per plant at soil level. Catches egg-laying adults within days. NOTE: Non-toxic. Replace when covered.
3. MOSQUITO BITS TEA — Soak bits per package directions, water plants with the tea. Bti bacteria kills larvae. NOTE: Bti targets fly larvae only — safe for plants, pets & people.
4. PEROXIDE DRENCH — 1 part 3% hydrogen peroxide : 4 parts water. Drench soil until it drains. NOTE: Kills larvae on contact. Use max 1x/week — it also kills helpful microbes.
5. TOP-DRESS BARRIER — Add 1/2 inch of sand or perlite on the soil surface. Keeps the top dry. NOTE: Physical barrier — adults can't reach soil to lay eggs.
Footer: Plant safety: the peroxide drench is safe for most houseplants but test on one plant first. Never exceed 1x/week.

pages.scope: The full sequence for fungus gnats in houseplants: confirm the pest (and tell it from a fruit fly or drain fly), let the top of the soil dry and by how much, yellow sticky traps for adults, a Bti drench (the 'mosquito bit tea' method: give the steeping method and amount only as an extension source or the product label gives it), a hydrogen peroxide drench with the EXACT ratio a source gives and an honest statement of how well it is supported, and when to repot. The life cycle timing that explains why treatment must run for weeks. Plant-safety notes for each step. A printable watering-schedule card. Pet and child notes for Bti, peroxide and sticky traps. This guide covers the method for any reader; the existing page on the site covers products sold in Canada, so link to it and do not repeat it.

pages.keyword: how to get rid of aphids naturally
pages.h1Hint: How to Get Rid of Aphids Naturally

heroText.title: Aphid Control Guide — 7 natural ways, including the ant connection (label: GARDEN & HOUSEPLANT GUIDE)
items: APHID: Pear-shaped, 1–4mm. Clusters on new growth & leaf undersides. NOT WHITEFLY: Whiteflies FLY in a cloud when disturbed — aphids don't. NOT SPIDER MITE: Pinpoint-size, fine webbing on leaves — smaller than aphids.

6 NATURAL CONTROLS: 1 Blast with water — Hard jet on leaf undersides, 2x/week. Simplest fix there is. 2 Insecticidal soap — Coat colonies directly. Repeat every 5–7 days, 3 rounds. 3 Neem oil at dusk — Disrupts feeding. Never on open blooms — bees first. 4 Release ladybugs — Release at dusk on damp plants near the colony. 5 Prune & trash — Cut the worst colonies, bag them; don't compost. 6 Invite hoverflies — Plant alyssum & dill nearby. Their larvae devour aphids.
NEEM SOAP SPRAY RECIPE: 1 tbsp neem oil : 1 tsp dish soap : 1 quart water. Shake well, coat leaf undersides at dusk. Use within 8 hours.
THE ANT CONNECTION: Ants FARM aphids — protecting them from ladybugs in exchange for honeydew. See ants on the plant? Control the ants and the aphids lose their bodyguards.
Footer: Safety: test soaps & neem on 2 leaves first. Spray at dusk to protect pollinators; keep away from kids & pets.

The ant and aphid relationship: why ants farm aphids for honeydew and why controlling the ants helps. Plant-safety and pollinator notes. Pet and child notes for soap and oil sprays.

pages.keyword: how to get rid of whiteflies
pages.h1Hint: How to Get Rid of Whiteflies: Identification and Natural Control

heroText.title: Whiteflies: Beat Them Naturally — ID them right, then break the cycle (label: GARDEN & HOUSEPLANT GUIDE)
items: WHITEFLY: Tiny white moth-like flies, ~2mm. THE SHAKE TEST: tap the plant — a white cloud rises = whiteflies. Cluster UNDER leaves; sticky honeydew.
VS APHID: Pear-shaped soft bodies, 1–4mm. Cluster on STEMS & new growth. Most don't fly — they crawl. Ants 'farm' them for honeydew.

WHY THEY'RE HARD TO KILL: One female lays 200+ eggs — mostly UNDER leaves where sprays miss. Eggs hatch in 5–10 days: you must repeat treatment 3x. Honeydew causes black sooty mold — treat early, not late.

6 NATURAL CONTROLS: 1 Yellow sticky traps — Hang at canopy height. Catches adults, breaks breeding. 2 Blast with water — Strong jet under leaves, 2x/week. Knocks off eggs & nymphs. 3 Insecticidal soap — Coat leaf undersides. Repeat every 5–7 days x3. 4 Neem oil spray — Disrupts feeding & reproduction. Apply at dusk. 5 Prune hotspots — Bag & trash heavily infested leaves; don't compost. 6 Reflective mulch — Silver mulch confuses incoming adults in veg gardens.
POLLINATOR RULE: Spray soaps & neem at DUSK, never on open blooms. Bees sleep at night — your spray won't touch them.
Footer: Safety: keep neem & soaps off skin/eyes; store away from kids & pets. Test any spray on 2 leaves first.

pages.scope: Whitefly identification and how to tell whiteflies from aphids, mealybugs and fungus gnats (a comparison table). The 'shake the plant' test. The life cycle and why the undersides of leaves matter. Five to seven natural controls in order: yellow sticky traps, a strong water spray, vacuuming adults in the cool of the morning, reflective mulch, insecticidal soap and horticultural or neem oil with the dilution a university source or the label gives, removing heavily infested leaves, and natural enemies. Why broad-spectrum insecticides make whiteflies worse. A printable cheat-sheet card. Plant-safety, pollinator, pet and child notes.

pages.h1Hint: Natural Weed Killer: What Works, With Exact Ratios and Honest Limits

heroText.title: Natural Weed Control — What works, exact ratios, honest limits (label: LAWN & GARDEN)
items: THE 3-INGREDIENT WEED KILLER: 1 gal vinegar (20%) : 1 cup salt : 1 tbsp dish soap. Mix in a pump sprayer. Spray on a HOT, sunny day — heat activates it. Kills top growth in hours. Deep-rooted weeds (dandelions) need 2–3 rounds. HONEST LIMITS: Salt sterilizes soil — use ONLY where nothing should grow (paths, driveways).
1. Boiling water — Pour on weeds in cracks & pavers. Instant, free, zero residue.
2. Smother with mulch — 3–4 inches of wood chips blocks light. Weeds can't sprout in the dark. (Diagram: 3–4 in of mulch over soil. Under 2 inches, light gets through.)
3. Pull after rain — Wet soil releases roots whole. Get the crown or it regrows.
4. Corn gluten meal — Pre-emergent: stops weed SEEDS sprouting. Pet-safe lawn option.
TIMING MATTERS: Spray vinegar at midday sun — heat + UV do the killing. No rain for 24h after spraying, or it washes off. Corn gluten goes down in EARLY spring, before weed seeds wake.
Footer: Pet-safe reminder: vinegar & boiling water are pet-safe once dry. Salt areas are NOT — keep pets off until rinsed.

pages.h1Hint: No-See-Ums: What They Are, Where They Live and How to Keep Them Out

pages.h1Hint: Cellar Spiders (Daddy Long Legs): Do They Bite, and How to Tell a Harvestman
pages.scope: Cellar spiders (family Pholcidae) for US and Canadian readers: the spider most people mean by "daddy long legs" indoors, identification and the bite question first. The quick answer: a tiny pale body on very long, thin legs, hanging upside down in a loose web in a basement, crawl space, garage or ceiling corner, that vibrates in its web until it blurs when disturbed, and that is not known to bite people (Penn State; UMN). Sizes only from sources (Penn State's long-bodied cellar spider: body about 1/4 to 5/16 inch, a female's front legs about 2 inches). The species people meet, each only as a source covers it: the long-bodied cellar spider, the most common of its family in the US (Penn State), the marbled cellar spider, which has displaced it in California (UC IPM), and the short-bodied cellar spider. "Cellar spider bite" and "are daddy long legs poisonous" answered at the sources' strength: Penn State says cellar spiders are not known to bite people; the story that they are the most venomous spider but cannot bite has no scientific basis, and harvestmen have no venom glands or fangs (UC Riverside's daddy-long-legs page; Missouri Dept. of Conservation); never a bite photo, never a diagnosis (bites in general: /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like). "Cellar spider vs harvestman" gets its own h2 and the quick-ID table (traits as rows: body parts, eyes, silk and web, legs, where you find it, venom), from the sources: a harvestman has one oval body with no waist, two eyes and no silk (MDC), a cellar spider two body parts, a cluster of eyes and a messy web (Penn State, MDC). The third "daddy longlegs", the crane fly, gets one card and one line that link /blog/mosquito-hawk-explained, which keeps every crane fly search. Then the female carrying her eggs in her jaws (one line; /blog/spider-egg-sacs), what cellar spiders eat (only as a source says; answer "do daddy long legs eat silverfish" only if one does), why they live indoors all year, and what to do: leave them, or remove webs with a broom or vacuum (UMN); control goes to /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-spiders (planned) or /blog/house-spiders. Cards: harvestman, crane fly, common house spider (/blog/house-spiders), brown recluse ("cellar spider vs brown recluse" stays with /blog/brown-recluse-look-alikes: one line and a link), camel cricket (/blog/camel-crickets, the long-legged basement jumper called a spider cricket). Link /tools/spider-identifier as the next step. Sources: Penn State Extension (long-bodied cellar spider), UMN Extension, UC IPM, UC Riverside (Vetter), Missouri Dept. of Conservation, as already cited on /blog/house-spiders, /blog/venomous-spiders, /blog/spiders-in-california and /tools/spider-identifier. No pesticide advice; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

pages.h1Hint: Carpet Beetle Bites: Why Carpet Beetles Don't Bite, and What the Rash Looks Like
pages.scope: Re-aimed to the searcher's words, "carpet beetle bites". The answer first: carpet beetles do not bite; the itchy, bite-like bumps some people get are a reaction to the larvae's hairs (carpet beetle dermatitis), as Penn State Extension, Texas A&M AgriLife and the CDC's Emerging Infectious Diseases report say, and most people never react (at the sources' strength). A quick-ID table under the quick answer: carpet beetle rash vs bed bug bites vs flea bites vs scabies vs mosquito bites: what it looks like, where on the body, when it appears, the sign to look for, each cell from a source (CDC, AAD or a medical school for the bites). What the rash looks like (red, itchy bumps or welts, often under clothing or where skin touched bedding or upholstery; never diagnose), who reacts (an acquired allergy, as Penn State says), how to confirm it (find the larvae and their cast skins: link /blog/signs-of-carpet-beetles and /blog/carpet-beetle-larvae), relief at the sources' strength (wash, launder bedding, an over-the-counter anti-itch cream only if a medical source names it), when to see a doctor (spreading or infected skin, eye or breathing symptoms, or no larvae found: scabies and other causes need a clinician), and the fix in one short section linking /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-carpet-beetles. Cards: carpet beetle larva (/blog/carpet-beetle-larvae), bites but no bed bugs (/blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs), bed bug bites and flea bites (no link until the US pages are live), scabies (no link). Never write that carpet beetles bite, burrow into skin or live on people. Sources: Penn State Extension (Carpet Beetle Dermatitis), CDC EID 2021 (Anthrenus dermatitis cluster), Texas A&M AgriLife, UC IPM, University of Kentucky, AAD or a medical school for bite care. The quick answer: what makes a jumping spider (two very large forward-facing eyes, a compact hairy body and short legs; it hunts by sight and pounces instead of waiting in a catching web), sizes only from sources, and that bites are uncommon and minor, at the sources' strength (a bite can happen when one is pressed or handled; none of the common species is treated as medically important by the extension sources). The species people meet, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the bold jumping spider (Phidippus audax: black with a white or orange spot pattern and iridescent green or blue jaws), Johnson's jumping spider (red abdomen, mainly in the West), the zebra jumping spider (Salticus scenicus, black-and-white striped, on house walls) and others only where a source and a photo exist; patterns vary within a species (Colorado State). Where and when they turn up indoors (sunny windows; they wander in and do not infest a house), what they eat (other insects, as sources say), and babies: spiderlings look like small adults; the silk retreat and egg sac only as sources describe them, linking /blog/spider-egg-sacs. The bite section: what a bite is like and when to get care, from CDC/NIOSH or extension pages, never diagnosing a wound as a spider bite, linking /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like (frozen until Oct 30: link only). pages.h1Hint: Yellow Sac Spiders: The Pale White Spider in the House, and Its Bite
pages.scope: Yellow sac spiders (Cheiracanthium) for US and Canadian readers, and for the reader who searched "white house spider" or "sac spider": a small, pale yellow to cream spider, sometimes greenish, with darker jaws and foot tips (Penn State), about 1/5 to 2/5 inch (UMN; Penn State gives females as 3/16 to 3/8 inch), that hunts at night on walls and ceilings without a web and hides by day in a flat silk sac in a wall-ceiling corner or behind shelves and pictures, dropping to the floor when disturbed (UC IPM). The quick answer bolds the tell: a pale spider that spends the day inside a small silk sac in a corner. The two common species, the agrarian (American) yellow sac spider and the longlegged (northern) yellow sac spider, which Penn State says is found mostly in buildings and lays its eggs almost exclusively indoors; where each lives in the US and Canada only as sources give it. A pale-spider sorter for the "white house spider" search (no source uses it as a species name): a quick-ID table, one row per pale spider people find indoors (yellow sac spider; cellar spider, linking /blog/daddy-long-legs; others only where a source supports them, for example a freshly molted spider or a white crab spider carried in on flowers), with size, color, web or sac, where you find it and the tell. Bites at the evidence's strength: Penn State says the two common sac spiders account for a significant number of bites, usually when one is trapped against skin in bedding, clothing or shoes, painful and burning at first with redness and swelling, normally without serious medical problems; studies of verified bites did not find the dying-tissue wounds once blamed on them (Vetter and colleagues' 20 verified bites, as /blog/venomous-spiders cites them); when to see a doctor only at a medical source's strength (CDC or a state health department); never diagnose from a photo (link /blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like and /tools/bug-bite-identifier). "Yellow sac spider vs brown recluse" stays with /blog/brown-recluse-look-alikes: a two-sentence section and a link. Then when they come indoors (the season only as a source gives it), the retreat and egg sac (/blog/spider-egg-sacs), and what to do: shake out clothes and shoes, vacuum the silk sacs, seal gaps (sources only); control goes to /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-spiders (planned). Cards: cellar spider, brown recluse, common house spider (/blog/house-spiders, which keeps "house spider"), false widow. Link /tools/spider-identifier as the next step. Sources: Penn State Extension (agrarian and longlegged sac spiders), UC IPM, UMN Extension, the verified-bite study, CDC or a state health department for care. No pesticide advice; no quote prompt (a traffic page).

pages.h1Hint: Paper Wasps: How to Identify Them, Their Umbrella Nests and How Bad the Sting Is
pages.scope: Paper wasps (Polistes) for US and Canadian readers, identification first. The quick answer: slender wasps that let their long hind legs dangle in flight, brown, reddish or black-and-yellow by species, that build a single open comb of paper cells hanging from one stalk with no outer cover (the "umbrella" nest under eaves, porch ceilings, railings, shutters and play sets); less defensive than yellowjackets but they sting to defend the nest, at the sources' strength. The species, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the European paper wasp (Polistes dominula, black and yellow, often taken for a yellowjacket), the dark paper wasp (P. fuscatus), and red and other regional paper wasps only as sources list them. A quick-ID table under the quick answer (paper wasp, yellowjacket, bald-faced hornet, European hornet, mud dauber): color, body and waist, legs in flight, nest type and place, how defensive, sting. The nest through the year (started by one queen in spring, largest in late summer, abandoned in fall and not reused, as sources say) and why a nest by a door is a problem while one on a far corner can often be left (they hunt caterpillars: their value as predators at the sources' strength). The sting: what it does, first aid and when to get emergency care (an allergic reaction, many stings), from CDC/NIOSH, the American Academy of Dermatology or Mayo Clinic; link bee-sting-vs-wasp-sting once live. Removing a nest: when to leave it, when and how to remove it only as extension sources describe (after dark or early morning, protective clothing, a product labeled for wasps: the label is the law; never a homemade spray, fire or water), and when to call a professional (a nest out of reach, anyone allergic). Cards: yellowjacket (yellow-jackets, no link until live), mud dauber (mud-daubers, same release), bald-faced hornet (bald-faced-hornets), European hornet (european-hornets). Sources: Penn State Extension, Clemson HGIC, University of Kentucky, UC IPM, Texas A&M AgriLife, Missouri Department of Conservation, CDC/NIOSH (insects). pages.scope: Assassin bugs (family Reduviidae) for US and Canadian readers, the wheel bug first because it is the one people find and photograph most (the cog-wheel crest on its back), identification first. The species, each with a photo where the ledger has one: the wheel bug (Arilus cristatus) adult and its bright red-and-black nymphs, the milkweed assassin bug (Zelus longipes), the masked hunter (Reduvius personatus, the one that comes indoors, its nymphs camouflaged in dust and lint) and others only where a source and a photo exist. A quick-ID table under the quick answer (wheel bug, milkweed assassin bug, masked hunter, kissing bug, leaf-footed bug, western conifer seed bug): size, color and shape, beak, where found, bites or not. The bite: what it feels like and what to do, from extension and medical sources at their strength, never "dangerous" beyond what they say; Chagas disease only as CDC states which bugs carry the parasite (CDC's look-alike page names the wheel bug among bugs that do not), linking kissing-bugs and chagas-disease once live. pages.h1Hint: Booklice (Psocids): The Tiny Pale Bugs in Damp Rooms, Books and Pantries
pages.scope: Booklice (psocids; indoors mostly Liposcelis) for US and Canadian readers who find tiny, pale, soft bugs on a windowsill, in a box of old books or papers, on cereal or flour packages, or in a new or damp house. The quick answer: tiny (sizes only from sources), wingless, grayish to translucent, quick-moving, with a large head; not true lice; they do not bite people or pets, and they feed on microscopic mold, so they are a sign of high humidity (each at the sources' strength). The common kinds, briefly (booklice indoors; winged barklice outdoors and on houseplants), with photos at a printed scale. Where they turn up and why: books and papers, wallpaper paste, stored food and pantry packages, new homes with damp plaster or drywall, basements, after a leak (as sources say). "Booklice in bed" and "booklice vs bed bugs": booklice do not feed on blood; how to tell them from bed bug nymphs, linking /blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs. Getting rid of them, humidity first, in order: dehumidify, ventilate, fix leaks, dry or discard moldy items, clean shelves, throw out infested food; insecticides only as sources say (they describe them as rarely needed). pages.h1Hint: Springtails: The Tiny Jumping Bugs in Bathrooms, Basements and Plant Soil
pages.scope: Springtails (Collembola) for US readers who find tiny jumping bugs indoors, identification first. The quick answer: tiny (sizes only from sources, inches first), soft-bodied and wingless, white, gray, black or banded, and they flip into the air with a forked, tail-like spring folded under the body; they need moisture and are a sign of it, and they do not bite people or damage the house (Colorado State, UMN, Penn State, UC IPM, whichever say so). The two body shapes people see (long-bodied and round, globular springtails) with photos at a printed scale. Where they turn up and why: tubs, sinks and shower drains, damp basements and window sills, wet potting soil after watering, pool water, and outdoors in mulch and leaf litter, sometimes in large numbers by foundations (each only as a source says); snow fleas, the springtails that dot late-winter snow, in one short section (a winter search). "Baby springtails": young springtails look like small adults (no larval stage), only as a source says. "Springtail or flea?" in one short section that links /blog/bugs-that-look-like-fleas, which keeps "springtails vs fleas"; the tiny-black-bug and houseplant searches stay with /blog/tiny-black-bugs and /blog/houseplant-bugs (link both). How to get rid of springtails, moisture first, in order: fix leaks and drips, ventilate the bathroom, run a dehumidifier, let houseplant soil dry between waterings, pull mulch and leaf litter back from the foundation, seal gaps, vacuum the ones indoors (Colorado State, UMN); insecticides only at the sources' strength (Colorado State advises avoiding them indoors where possible; UMN says there are no pesticides for springtails in houseplants), never a home-remedy spray. Quick-ID table: the springtail and its look-alikes (flea, booklouse, mite, fungus gnat larva in soil), one row each: size, color, how it moves, where you find it, bites or not. Cards: flea (/blog/bugs-that-look-like-fleas), booklouse (no link: /blog/booklice is slated for replacement), silverfish (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-silverfish), fungus gnat (/learn/how-to-get-rid-of-fungus-gnats). pages.h1Hint: Mice in Walls: Scratching Sounds, Signs and How to Get Them Out
pages.scope: The page for the reader who hears something in the wall, identification first: what is in the wall, by sound, time and sign. Scratching, scurrying and squeaking at night (mice: Nebraska); rats, mainly roof rats, which nest in attics and wall voids (UC IPM); noise by day from gray squirrels and at night from flying squirrels (as /blog/animals-in-attic sorts them, UGA); squeaking and chattering around dusk (bats: USFWS); a faint rustling (carpenter ants: UC IPM); and the insects that winter in wall voids and wander out on warm days (/blog/bugs-in-house-in-winter). Quick-ID table, one row per suspect: what you hear, when, the droppings, the other sign. For each suspect a photo, the sign that confirms it (droppings and their size, a musky smell, gnaw marks, dark rub marks at holes and along pipes, shredded nesting material; NPS Conserve O Gram 3/12 shows mouse signs) and a link (/blog/rat-vs-mouse, /blog/roof-rat-vs-norway-rat, /blog/animals-in-attic, /blog/bat-poop, /blog/mouse-poop, /blog/mouse-urine). Then how mice get into and travel through walls (openings of 1/4 inch, along pipes, wires and sill plates; climbing goes to /blog/can-mice-climb-walls) and how to get them out without sealing them in: snap traps where they leave the wall (behind the stove and refrigerator, under sinks, where pipes enter, above drop ceilings: CDC, Nebraska; trap types go to /blog/mice-traps), traps set and working before the last holes are closed and a week with no catches before calling it done (CDC, consistent with /blog/fall-mouse-proofing-checklist and /blog/steel-wool-for-mice), and why poison and ultrasonic devices are a poor fit for wall voids (UC IPM, Cornell, Nebraska; /blog/mice-poison). A dead mouse in the wall: why it happens, how long the smell lasts (Cornell: days for a mouse), when opening the wall is worth it; finding and removing the carcass stays on /blog/mice-removal. When to call a pro: /blog/mice-exterminator. Health only from CDC at its strength (never sweep or vacuum droppings or nests; hantavirus and which mice carry it: /blog/deer-mice). Sources: CDC rodent control (seal up, trap up, clean up), EPA, Nebraska Extension G1105, UC IPM Pest Notes (house mouse, rats, carpenter ants), Cornell, Penn State, Purdue, NPS Conserve O Gram 3/12, the USFWS bat manual, UGA. pages.h1Hint: Flea Dirt: What Flea Poop Looks Like on Dogs and Cats, and How to Test It
pages.scope: The flea dirt page, identification first: what flea dirt is (the digested blood adult fleas excrete as they feed: Ohio State, Texas A&M, the University of Florida's cat flea profile, Penn State's cat flea fact sheet), what it looks like at life size and magnified (black to reddish-black specks like ground pepper, comma-shaped up close: the University of Minnesota's veterinary diagnostics textbook, the Merck Veterinary Manual; a size only if a source gives one), and the wet paper towel test as the centerpiece, step by step: comb the pet over white paper, a white sink or a pillowcase, put the specks on a damp white paper towel, and flea dirt dissolves into reddish-brown smears where ordinary dirt does not (Ohio State, Minnesota, Merck, Cornell Feline Health Center). Where to look: on a dog, the neck, shoulder blades and base of the tail, belly and groin (Ohio State, Minnesota, Merck); on a cat, the back of the neck, the top of the tail head, belly and back (Cornell Feline Health Center); with a fine-toothed flea comb; then pet bedding, resting spots, beds and carpet, and for cats shelves and tabletops (Ohio State). A photo strip and quick-ID table, flea dirt vs ordinary dirt vs flea eggs vs dandruff, and look-alike cards (flea eggs; bed bug poop, which also runs red but stains mattress seams; cockroach specks). What finding it means: adult fleas are feeding on the animal now, even when none is seen (Merck: dogs very allergic to flea saliva may be almost free of fleas because they groom so much), and larvae develop where flea dirt collects because they feed on it (only as UF, UC IPM and Penn State put it); flea dirt but no fleas; flea dirt in a bed. Whether it is harmful, at the sources' strength: CDC's flea-borne typhus page (infected flea dirt rubbed into bites or other wounds; murine-typhus once live) and cat-scratch disease page (scratches contaminated with flea feces), anemia in heavily infested kittens and puppies (Cornell, Merck), tapeworm (Texas A&M, Cornell). What to do: treat every pet with a product a veterinarian recommends, never a dog product on a cat (Cornell; CDC: never permethrin on cats), wash pet bedding hot and vacuum often (UC IPM), then /blog/how-to-get-rid-of-fleas for the full plan; no product advice here. Not a second eggs page: eggs, larvae and cocoons stay with /blog/flea-eggs (one short section and a link), the adult flea with /blog/what-do-fleas-look-like. pages.h1Hint: Camel Crickets (Spider Crickets): How to Identify Them and Get Rid of Them
pages.scope: Camel crickets for US and Canadian readers, identification first: a humpbacked, wingless cricket, light tan to dark brown, with antennae much longer than its body and large hind legs, that never chirps (no sound-making organs, per Clemson HGIC; chirping indoors points to field crickets, per NC State) and jumps a surprisingly long way (MDC); sizes only from sources (Clemson: 1/2 to 1 1/2 inches; MDC: body up to about 1 inch). The "jumps at you" reputation only as a source puts it: NC State, Clemson and MDC do not say they jump toward people, and it is never an attack. Which ones get into homes: the greenhouse camel cricket (Tachycines asynamorus, also written Diestrammena asynamora), the most common camel cricket in eastern US homes (Epps et al. 2014, PeerJ; NC State), and the native camel or cave crickets (Ceuthophilus); nymphs look like small adults (NC State). Then the "spider cricket" question, spider or cricket (six legs and long antennae against a spider's eight legs and none), with look-alike cards: house and field cricket (crickets-in-house, once live), cellar spider (/blog/house-spiders), wolf spider (/blog/wolf-spiders), house centipede (/blog/house-centipedes). Where they live and why they come in: damp basements, crawl spaces, garages and laundry rooms; outdoors under stones, logs, firewood, mulch and ivy; large numbers point to a moisture problem (MDC); whether they breed indoors, where sources differ (MDC and Iowa State: unlikely unless it stays dark and damp; Cornell's Nassau County office: they can). Bites and harm at the sources' strength: none of the sources read reports a bite (MDC and Kentucky call them harmless); damage only as Clemson (fine fabrics and houseplants when numerous) and NC State (stored garments and linens after a long infestation; dark fecal smears on joists) put it. A control section, since this page owns "how to get rid of camel crickets": dry the space, seal and weather-strip, pull mulch, firewood and stored boxes back from walls, sticky traps in corners and behind appliances, vacuum (NC State, Clemson); insecticides only as those sources put them (perimeter first, baits in crawl spaces, a product labeled for the site; the label is the law), no product names. One line each, linked once live: chirping crickets (crickets-in-house) and the unrelated desert camel spider (camel-spiders); the western Jerusalem cricket is another family (UC IPM), one line at most. Sources: NC State Extension's Camel Crickets (revised 2023), Clemson HGIC, University of Maryland Extension, University of Kentucky, MDC, Iowa State, Epps et al. 2014.

pages.h1Hint: Bed Bugs in Hotels: How to Check Your Room and Avoid Bringing Them Home
pages.scope: For US travelers, the hotel check first, in the order to do it. Keep luggage off the floor and off the bed until the check is done, on a luggage rack, table or other hard surface (University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636; EPA's Protecting Your Home from Bed Bugs says to inspect the luggage rack). Check the bed from the pillow end with a flashlight: sheets and pillows back, mattress seams, piping and tags, and the box spring where it can be seen (Kentucky); the headboard edges and the gap behind it, a frequent hiding place in hotel rooms, without taking it down (Kentucky warns untrained people not to); then the nightstand, upholstered chairs and the luggage rack straps. What the signs look like in a hotel bed (live bugs, ink-dot fecal spots, shed skins, eggs), with photos at life size, linking /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist, /blog/bed-bug-poop and /blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like; why a clean check is not proof (Virginia Tech: in a new infestation, a hotel room for example, evidence can be very hard to find). If you find them: tell the front desk, ask for a room in a different part of the hotel because infestations sometimes extend to nearby units (Kentucky), photograph the evidence and keep luggage closed; who must act is set by states and cities, not EPA (EPA's Bed Bug Laws and Regulations page: 21 states with some law or regulation, focused mostly on hotels and landlords), stated at that strength, no legal advice. Bites during or after a trip: marks can take as long as 14 days to show and bites alone do not confirm bed bugs (CDC), and bites noticed after getting home do not mean the home is infested (Virginia Tech); link /blog/bed-bug-bites and /blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs. Coming home: unpack away from the bedroom, put clothing straight into the washer or dryer (heat settings only as a source gives them), heat-treat or isolate a suitcase you are worried about (Kentucky: a hot car in summer; Rutgers: a portable heating box), why Kentucky rates inspecting or vacuuming a suitcase as less useful, how to watch for bed bugs at home afterwards (interceptors under the bed legs; /blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist) and what to do if they came home (/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs). For perspective, Kentucky says most hotel infestations are limited to a few rooms. A where-to-check table (spot, what to look for, how to check it) and look-alike cards (bat bug, carpet beetle larva, cockroach nymph, spider beetle; /blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs). Hiding places in general go to /blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide. Sources: EPA (How to Find Bed Bugs; Protecting Your Home from Bed Bugs; Bed Bug Laws and Regulations), CDC, University of Kentucky ENTFACT-636, Virginia Tech, Rutgers and the Indiana Department of Health, as already cited on /blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide and /learn/bed-bugs. Never name a hotel, chain, booking or registry site; no spray or product advice beyond the one generic pick; no quote prompt (a traffic page; BuzzSkito does not treat bed bugs).
